title: When Text-to-Image Helps Editing:The Effects of Conditioning During Denoising

paper.title: When Text-to-Image Helps Editing: The Effects of Conditioning During Denoising
paper.abstract: Abstract Unified models are trained for both instruction-based image editing and text-to-image (T2I) generation, but standard editing pipelines keep source-image conditioning throughout denoising. We ask whether editing can benefit from T2I, and study how the effects of conditioning vary across edits and denoising stages. In pure editing, source attention declines for some edits over the sampling trajectory. This observation led us to task switching, which lets the model draw on its T2I capabilities. Across three unified editors and four benchmarks, switching to the T2I task for bounded intervals improves edit quality, while mean perceptual preservation remains close to pure editing across all three models. Unified editors therefore benefit from using both conditioning modes they are trained for, and the timing of the switch sets the balance between quality and preservation.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: Switching conditioning helps added objects fit the scene. Adding two dogs to a blue-lit room with pure editing produces artifacts and mismatched lighting (orange close-up). Switching to caption-only T2I at k 1 k_{1} improves integration but changes the room. The E → T2I → E \mathrm{E}\to\mathrm{T2I}\to\mathrm{E} schedule returns to editing at k 2 k_{2} to retain more of the source. Unified multimodal models support text-to-image (T2I) generation and instruction-based image editing with the same architecture and weights ( Black Forest Labs, 2025 ; Deng et al., 2025 ) . T2I generation synthesizes an image from a caption describing the desired scene ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , while editing transforms a source image according to a natural-language instruction ( Brooks et al., 2023 ) . Within a unified model, the two tasks offer a synergy between synthesizing a coherent target scene and retaining relevant content from an existing image. Standard pipelines nevertheless use these capabilities separately. In diffusion editors such as FLUX2-Klein ( Black Forest Labs, 2025 ) , editing conditions on the source image and instruction throughout denoising, while T2I generation uses a caption alone. Source-image conditioning therefore stays fixed over the course of an edit, and the model’s dual capability goes unused within a single trajectory. Persistent source-image anchoring preserves structure, but it can also suppress intended changes ( Hertz et al., 2022 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ) . When the target scene diverges substantially from the input, editors can under-execute the instruction or integrate the change poorly, with visible seams and mismatched lighting. This raises a question: does every edit benefit from source-image conditioning at every stage of denoising? To answer it, we examine source-image attention in pure-editing trajectories. With source conditioning available throughout denoising, some edits progressively attend less to it, while localized changes retain strong source attention through the final steps ( Section 3.1 ). This led us to test whether temporarily removing source conditioning can improve edit fidelity and naturalness. For a fixed interval, we remove source-image conditioning and replace the editing instruction with a target caption generated by a vision-language model (VLM). We then restore the original editing inputs. The model weights and number of denoiser forward passes remain unchanged. Figure 1 shows an example: switching to T2I helps integrate the added objects into the scene, and returning to editing preserves more of the original room.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: • We find that the strength of source-image attention depends on the type of edit and varies over the course of denoising. This suggests that for some classes of edits, source conditioning is redundant at certain stages. • We identify a conditioning regime that consistently improves edit quality across three models and four benchmarks while keeping preservation virtually the same. • We vary the degrees of freedom of this regime, the conditioning inputs, the interval placement and duration, and the guidance formulation, and characterize how each affects edit quality and preservation.

sections.heading: Attention and source conditioning.
sections.text: Prompt-to-Prompt reuses cross-attention maps over text tokens from a source generation and limits their injection in time to permit structural changes ( Hertz et al., 2022 ) . SaaS identifies source-image dominance over neglected instructions in OmniGen and adaptively scales instruction attention. In its examples, jointly replacing image and text inputs late in denoising has little effect ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) . GRAG modulates the relative influence of source-image and instruction tokens to control editing intensity ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . We ask the same question about source conditioning, but instead of rescaling attention we change the conditioning inputs themselves and measure the outcome, using attention maps only as a diagnostic.

sections.heading: Temporal conditioning.
sections.text: eDiff-I observes that reliance on text conditioning decreases during sampling and trains separate denoisers for different noise levels ( Balaji et al., 2022 ) . Restricting classifier-free guidance to a limited interval also improves generation ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ) . PCI intervenes on the text prompt during T2I sampling to find when a concept can still be inserted. The resulting temporal profiles differ across concepts and models and carry over to editing ( Görgün et al., 2026 ) . We extend this line of work from varying denoisers, guidance, or text prompts across denoising stages to switching between image-conditioned editing and caption-only generation within a unified model.

sections.heading: Combining generation and editing.
sections.text: HiDream-E1’s released pipeline provides a direct precedent for an editing-to-generation handoff: it continues the same latent with a target caption, removes source-image conditioning, and finishes the remaining steps with the HiDream-I1 generator weights ( HiDream-ai, 2025 ) . For refinement of generated images, RvR argues that pixel-level preservation restricts the space of possible changes, and trains a regeneration model conditioned on target prompts and semantic image tokens without source VAE tokens ( Guo et al., 2026 ) . Building on these pipelines, we study how source-image conditioning, the text paired with it, and interval timing affect edit quality and source preservation across unified editors. Conditioning controls and timing sweeps use the models’ native editing and T2I modes within one denoising trajectory under unchanged weights.

sections.heading: 3 Source conditioning along editing trajectories
sections.text: A unified model is trained for two tasks but runs one at a time. Every editing request has a source image, and the pipeline conditions on it at every step regardless of what the request asks for. Editing requests, however, differ widely in nature and in difficulty: enhancing the lighting adjusts an intact scene, whereas replacing a background asks the model to synthesize most of the image from scratch. It would be surprising if one conditioning policy served both equally well. This section examines how an editor actually uses the source image across such edits and across denoising steps.

sections.heading: 3.1 Source attention varies across edits and timesteps
sections.text: If the source image matters more for some edits than for others, the most direct place to look is the model’s attention to it. We therefore measure how much each output patch attends to the source-image tokens during ordinary editing, and how that changes as denoising proceeds. We examine source attention along 50 50 -step pure-editing trajectories on FLUX2-Klein 4B. For each output latent patch i i , we sum attention over source-image tokens and average across heads and transformer blocks, obtaining a i a_{i} . At step k = 9 k=9 ( Figure 2 ), the three edits attend to the source very differently: only on the kept foreground for the background replacement, strongly everywhere for the lighting change, and weakly everywhere for the makeup look. How much the model uses the source depends on what the edit needs from it. Figure 2: Source attention varies across edits (FLUX2-Klein 4B, step 9). Maps average over heads and blocks. a i a_{i} @9 shows per-patch source attention; CV@9 shows the coefficient of variation in local 3 × 3 3\times 3 neighborhoods. Attention also changes over time ( Figure 3 a): source-attention mass generally decreases in the examined trajectories, whereas some local edits retain high attention through the final steps. The source image and instruction are identical at every step, so this variation reflects how the model uses fixed inputs. Where attention to the source has faded, conditioning on it constrains the model without contributing much. Since T2I generation is free of that constraint, we hypothesize that it can produce a better scene, and the question becomes where in the trajectory a T2I phase would disturb the edit the least.

sections.heading: 3.2 Comparing editing and T2I predictions
sections.text: The two conditioning modes propose different updates to the same latent. Where they agree, switching between them changes little; where they diverge, a switch pulls the trajectory off the edit. To find the low-disturbance region, we compute both predictions at every step of an ordinary edit. At each latent state of a pure-editing trajectory, we compare predictions conditioned on the source image and instruction ( v E v_{\mathrm{E}} ) with predictions conditioned on a target caption ( v T2I v_{\mathrm{T2I}} ). Their directional agreement and norm ratio ( Figure 3 b,c) are highly variable early, comparatively stable in the middle, and diverge again late for local edits. This suggests that the effect of switching depends on its timing, so we test both one-way switches and bounded intervals placed in the stable middle region. The comparison is a diagnostic: it reads both predictions at each step without altering the sampled trajectory, whereas the switching schedules below evaluate one mode per step. Figure 3: Conditioning disagreement and source attention along pure editing (FLUX2-Klein 4B). (a) Source-attention mass generally decreases, while local edits retain high attention late in sampling. (b) Prediction cosine similarity, initially low (median 0.48 0.48 ). (c) T2I/edit prediction norm ratio. Both are evaluated at identical latent states.

sections.heading: 4 Effects of conditioning and interval timing
sections.text: To test whether the effect is a property of unified editors rather than of one model, we evaluate three that differ in size, architecture, and training: FLUX2-Klein 4B and 9B ( Black Forest Labs, 2025 ) , two sizes of one diffusion-transformer family, and BAGEL ( Deng et al., 2025 ) , a separately developed model. The benchmarks cover complementary aspects of editing quality. GEdit-Bench ( Liu et al., 2025 ) uses real user instructions across task types and scores semantic consistency and perceptual quality separately. ImgEdit ( Ye et al., 2025 ) adds hard categories such as extraction, composition, and actions. MagicBrush ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) supplies a reference caption for every target, which allows a judge-free alignment score. GIE-Bench ( Qian et al., 2025 ) scores functional correctness and preservation separately, so quality gains can be priced in preservation.

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: All models run with unchanged weights and 50 50 steps ( k = 0 , … , 49 k=0,\ldots,49 ); target captions and improved instructions come from Gemini-2.5-pro by default ( Comanici et al., 2025 ) (Qwen3.5 captioners are compared in Appendix D ). GEdit is judged by GPT-4.1 ( OpenAI, 2025 ) on a 0 0 – 10 10 scale, ImgEdit by GPT-4o ( Hurst et al., 2024 ) on 1 1 – 5 5 , and GIE-Bench correctness by GPT-4o in % \% ; MagicBrush reports CLIP-T cosine similarity to the reference caption, and GIE-Bench preservation is SSIM outside the edit mask and whole-image Unmasked-CLIP similarity to the source. Per GEdit sample, semantic consistency (SC) is the minimum of fidelity and preservation, perceptual quality (PQ) the minimum of naturalness and artifact-free appearance, and overall O = SC ⋅ PQ O=\sqrt{\mathrm{SC}\cdot\mathrm{PQ}} ; scores are averaged within task types, then across types. The GEdit conditioning matrices and Figures 6 and 7 use Qwen3.5 ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) ; the extended 4B GIE-Bench sweep uses Gemini-3-Flash ( Google DeepMind, 2025 ) .

sections.heading: Variability.
sections.text: Baseline standard deviations come from three seeds with one judge pass each, so they mix generation and judge variability. They describe the baseline only, and the uncertainty of the switching gains is assessed separately. Paired quality tests on 4B use two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and exact McNemar tests for binary correctness on matched per-edit records. Preservation comparisons are described in Appendix F .

sections.heading: 4.1 Task switching improves editing quality
sections.text: Trading preservation for quality is easy: any editor can be pushed toward the target by loosening its anchor to the source. Improving quality without giving up preservation is the hard part, and this is what a T2I interval achieves. Our sweeps over interval length and position identify [ 10 , 16 ) [10,16) as a strong fixed interval: applied to every edit, it raises all six quality scores on all three models ( Table 2 ), while preservation as judged by GPT-4.1 stays within a fraction of a point of pure editing. The pixel-level measures, SSIM and Unmasked-CLIP, do drop, and Section 4.4 examines how much of that drop is perceptible. The interval is not unique: several placements improve GEdit semantic consistency and perceptual quality at once ( Figure 4 ), and which one is best depends on the model and the metric. We feature [ 10 , 16 ) [10,16) because it was consistently strong in the FLUX2-Klein 4B sweeps across all four benchmarks. On 9B and BAGEL we tested a smaller set of intervals, and [ 10 , 16 ) [10,16) again ranked among the strongest ( Figures 4 and 9 ), so we report it for all three models and use it for the selective variant. The interval was not re-tuned per model or benchmark. Full GIE-Bench, MagicBrush, and GEdit results are reported in Tables 3 , 4 and 5 . sections.heading: Image and text conditioning.
sections.text: Switching changes two things at once, the image input and the text, and the controls in Table 1 pull them apart; Table 8 summarizes the best scores for each conditioning schedule. Rewording alone does help: a VLM-improved instruction early in the trajectory reaches the highest GEdit overall score among the control winners ( Figure 7 , left). But the perceptual-quality gain is specific to removing the source image. With the same caption, comparing conditioning with and without the source image ( Figure 6 ) shows that removing the image allows larger gains in fidelity, naturalness, and artifact scores on every model. The text matters in two different ways. Removing the image while keeping only the editing instruction loses semantic consistency, because nothing tells the model what the scene should become. Pairing the caption with the source image also loses semantic consistency, whether the pair is used for the whole trajectory or only outside the interval; here the caption does describe the target, so the likely cause is that the editor was trained to combine the source image with an instruction, not with a description of the result. The improvement therefore comes from switching the task, source-free generation toward a described target, and not from either change alone. The strongest single competitor is the improved instruction used for the whole trajectory, pure E ∗ , which costs the same one VLM call and the same two denoiser passes per step as switching ( Table 10 ). It is a strong baseline on the two FLUX models, where it wins GEdit semantic consistency and keeps SSIM higher. But on every model the best T2I interval beats it on GIE-Bench functional correctness, MagicBrush alignment, and GEdit perceptual quality, and the perceptual-quality margin is large. Where E ∗ wins semantic consistency, it does so through the preservation part of that score; fidelity is matched or exceeded by the T2I interval. On BAGEL, the improved instruction alone does not help at all, while the T2I interval improves every quality score. Better prompts make the editor follow the instruction more faithfully; only switching makes the result look better. sections.heading: Continuous guidance comparisons.
sections.text: Continuous guidance provides a natural alternative to switching. Reducing image guidance over the same intervals barely changes GEdit overall and lowers ImgEdit, because image-conditioned predictions still drive the update even at zero guidance. Adding a caption-conditioned branch instead blends edit and T2I velocities at every step. At a quarter editing weight, this improves semantic consistency, correctness, and preservation over the pure E → T2I → E \mathrm{E}\to\mathrm{T2I}\to\mathrm{E} switch, but requires four denoiser passes per step rather than two ( Appendix C ). Switching is the endpoint of this family at the cost of pure editing and captures most of the benefit.

sections.heading: 4.3 When does switching help?
sections.text: Interval placement and duration are not independent knobs. Across all four durations, the sweeps trace one curve ( Figure 7 , right): moving an interval earlier or making it longer buys perceptual quality and spends semantic consistency, and every curve returns to the pure-editing point as the interval slides toward the end of the trajectory. What matters is how much of the trajectory is spent in T2I and how early. The semantic-consistency cost comes from its preservation half; because SC takes the per-sample minimum of fidelity and preservation, a fidelity gain is hidden whenever preservation drops further. Only short intervals in the early-middle of the trajectory land in the region that improves both scores, which is why [ 10 , 16 ) [10,16) is the featured setting. Beyond that region the choice is a trade: an editor that values naturalness should switch earlier or longer, one that values consistency later or shorter. sections.heading: 4.4 Quality and source preservation
sections.text: The quality gains are not free, but the two kinds of preservation metric price them very differently. SSIM outside the edit mask and Unmasked-CLIP drop for every switching configuration, and significantly so ( Appendix F ). A judge asked only about unintended changes sees far less. We score preservation with GPT-4.1 using GEdit’s preservation criterion with the fidelity part removed, so the judge penalizes only changes that the instruction did not ask for ( Appendix F ). On this measure the fixed interval moves mean preservation by at most 0.16 0.16 points on a ten-point scale across the three models, and none of these shifts is significant. Figure 8 (right) puts the two sides together: the featured intervals gain correctness at judged preservation indistinguishable from pure editing, while the early one-way switches that gain the most correctness are the ones that pay for it. Withholding the interval from part of the edits ( Section 4.5 ) recovers a portion of the SSIM loss on every model and brings judged preservation closer still to pure editing. Figure 8: Preservation and correctness on GIE-Bench (FLUX2-Klein 4B). Left: mean GPT-4.1 preservation versus SSIM outside the edit mask; shading: near-baseline plateau; faint curve: visual guide. Pearson r r is computed separately below and above SSIM 0.76 0.76 . Right: Gemini-3-Flash correctness versus mean GPT preservation with 95 % 95\% source-clustered confidence intervals ( Appendix F ). The two metrics disagree because they measure different things. Figure 8 (left) shows how far the pixel drop overstates the cost: across the 4B sweep, judged preservation forms a plateau at the pure-editing level while SSIM varies, and declines only below it. SSIM is known to fall sharply under small translations, rescaling, or rotations that leave an image perceptually unchanged ( Wang & Simoncelli, 2005 ; Ding et al., 2022 ) , and regenerating a scene from a caption for a few steps is likely to introduce exactly such shifts. SSIM therefore tracks pixel displacement, while the instruction-aware judge is the closer estimate of what a viewer would notice.

sections.heading: 4.5 Selective application as an illustration
sections.text: Section 3.1 showed that source attention reflects how much an edit still depends on the source. Read at the step before the interval, the same signal can decide whether to switch: edits that still depend on the source are more likely to be hurt by removing it. As an illustrative application, we summarize source attention at k = 9 k=9 by its strength and its spatial unevenness: π = Q 0.75 ​ ( { a i } ) , cv = σ ⁡ ( { a i } ) / μ ⁡ ( { a i } ) . \pi=Q_{0.75}(\{a_{i}\}),\qquad\mathrm{cv}=\sigma(\{a_{i}\})/\mu(\{a_{i}\}). (1) Edits with strong or uneven source attention stay in pure editing; the rest are switched. Both statistics come from the ordinary edit pass at no extra denoiser cost. Thresholds were tuned on GEdit outcomes for 4B and on GEdit probe distributions for 9B and BAGEL, then shared across all benchmarks ( Appendix E ). Selection does what it was meant to do. It keeps the quality gain over pure editing on every score and every model ( Table 2 ), and relative to the fixed interval it moves the operating point toward preservation: SSIM improves significantly on all three models and judged preservation moves closer to pure editing, at the price of somewhat smaller quality gains. The natural question is whether the attention rule is better than choosing edits at random. In a counterfactual replay on GEdit we therefore compare the rule with random routing tuned to spend the same mean preservation ( Appendix E ). The rule wins on 4B and, with thresholds transferred by matching probe distributions alone, again on 9B: at equal preservation it delivers higher overall, perceptual-quality, and fidelity scores. The attention signal identifies edits that can afford the interval.

sections.heading: 5 Discussion and conclusion
sections.text: Unified editors are trained for two tasks but use one at a time; this study puts the unused mode to work within an edit. An editor’s attention to the source image depends on what the edit needs from it and fades over denoising for edits that rebuild the scene, leaving a stretch of the trajectory where source conditioning constrains without contributing. Switching to the model’s own T2I mode on that stretch improves edit quality on every model and benchmark we tested, while an instruction-aware judge finds preservation essentially unchanged. The gain is a property of the switch rather than of the prompt: removing the source image is what unlocks perceptual quality, the caption is what keeps the scene on target, and continuous guidance reproduces the effect only at twice the cost. Placement and duration set where on the quality–preservation curve an editor lands, and the same attention signal that motivated the study can decide per edit whether to switch at all. We use a simple switching schedule to establish that task switching can improve editing quality. More sophisticated switching and conditioning schemes may offer further gains. Our interval sweeps are coarse, so [ 10 , 16 ) [10,16) is one effective setting among those tested. A caption prepared before sampling cannot react to the trajectory, and its errors produce coherent but unintended changes. Preservation is measured by image similarity and a GPT judge, and how these track human judgments is untested.

sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.text: AI assistants helped implement switching conditions, perform statistical tests of preservation, prepare figures, search the literature, polish author-written text, and identify inconsistencies in reported numerical results. The authors verified citations, experimental code, and numerical outputs and take responsibility for the final text, claims, and artifacts.

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.text: Sections 3 and 4.5 specify the conditioning schedules and attention statistics, while Sections 4.1 and E describe interval selection and model-specific thresholds. The experimental setup and evaluation metrics are described in Section 4 , with extended results and guidance formulas in Appendices B and C . Appendix D reports captioner comparisons and timings, and Appendix F describes the preservation judge protocol. Generation code and example notebooks for all three models are available at https://github.com/pbnc5r6/conditioning-switching .

sections.heading: Appendix C Continuous guidance comparisons
sections.text: On FLUX2-Klein 4B, we test whether lowering image guidance reproduces the effect of a T2I interval, and introduce a multimodal guidance formulation that continuously combines editing with target-caption-conditioned generation. Let U U , T T , I I , and E E denote denoiser predictions conditioned on neither image nor text, the target caption alone, the source image alone, and the source image with the edit instruction, respectively.

sections.heading: Judge protocol.
sections.text: We use GPT-4.1, the same judge as in our main GEdit evaluation, providing the source image, edited image, and editing instruction. The prompt and scoring scale are adapted from GEdit’s semantic-consistency evaluation by retaining the preservation assessment and removing the fidelity assessment. The preservation-only prompt asks the judge to score unnecessary changes to unrelated content from 0 0 to 10 10 , without penalizing changes needed to carry out the instruction. A score of 0 0 indicates substantial unrelated changes; 10 10 indicates that all unrelated content is preserved.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.01681v1 [cs.CV] 01 Oct 2026 When Text-to-Image Helps Editing: The Effects of Conditioning During Denoising Lidia Troeshestova Affiliation: HSE University & Yandex Alexander Ustyuzhanin Affiliation: Yandex Sergey Kastryulin Affiliation: Yandex Abstract Unified models are trained for both instruction-based image editing and text-to-image (T2I) generation, but standard editing pipelines keep source-image conditioning throughout denoising. We ask whether editing can benefit from T2I, and study how the effects of conditioning vary across edits and denoising stages. In pure editing, source attention declines for some edits over the sampling trajectory. This observation led us to task switching, which lets the model draw on its T2I capabilities. Across three unified editors and four benchmarks, switching to the T2I task for bounded intervals improves edit quality, while mean perceptual preservation remains close to pure editing across all three models. Unified editors therefore benefit from using both conditioning modes they are trained for, and the timing of the switch sets the balance between quality and preservation. † † footnotetext: An earlier version of this work appeared as “DuET: Dual Expert Trajectories for Diffusion Image Editing” ( Troeshestova et al., 2026 ) (arXiv:2606.13303). 1 Introduction Figure 1: Switching conditioning helps added objects fit the scene. Adding two dogs to a blue-lit room with pure editing produces artifacts and mismatched lighting (orange close-up). Switching to caption-only T2I at k 1 k_{1} improves integration but changes the room. The E → T2I → E \mathrm{E}\to\mathrm{T2I}\to\mathrm{E} schedule returns to editing at k 2 k_{2} to retain more of the source. Unified multimodal models support text-to-image (T2I) generation and instruction-based image editing with the same architecture and weights ( Black Forest Labs, 2025 ; Deng et al., 2025 ) . T2I generation synthesizes an image from a caption describing the desired scene ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , while editing transforms a source image according to a natural-language instruction ( Brooks et al., 2023 ) . Within a unified model, the two tasks offer a synergy between synthesizing a coherent target scene and retaining relevant content from an existing image. Standard pipelines nevertheless use these capabilities separately. In diffusion editors such as FLUX2-Klein ( Black Forest Labs, 2025 ) , editing conditions on the source image and instruction throughout denoising, while T2I generation uses a caption alone. Source-image conditioning therefore stays fixed over the course of an edit, and the model’s dual capability goes unused within a single trajectory. Persistent source-image anchoring preserves structure, but it can also suppress intended changes ( Hertz et al., 2022 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ) . When the target scene diverges substantially from the input, editors can under-execute the instruction or integrate the change poorly, with visible seams and mismatched lighting. This raises a question: does every edit benefit from source-image conditioning at every stage of denoising? To answer it, we examine source-image attention in pure-editing trajectories. With source conditioning available throughout denoising, some edits progressively attend less to it, while localized changes retain strong source attention through the final steps ( Section 3.1 ). This led us to test whether temporarily removing source conditioning can improve edit fidelity and naturalness. For a fixed interval, we remove source-image conditioning and replace the editing instruction with a target caption generated by a vision-language model (VLM). We then restore the original editing inputs. The model weights and number of denoiser forward passes remain unchanged. Figure 1 shows an example: switching to T2I helps integrate the added objects into the scene, and returning to editing preserves more of the original room. Contributions. • We find that the strength of source-image attention depends on the type of edit and varies over the course of denoising. This suggests that for some classes of edits, source conditioning is redundant at certain stages. • We identify a conditioning regime that consistently improves edit quality across three models and four benchmarks while keeping preservation virtually the same. • We vary the degrees of freedom of this regime, the conditioning inputs, the interval placement and duration, and the guidance formulation, and characterize how each affects edit quality and preservation. 2 Related Work Attention and source conditioning. Prompt-to-Prompt reuses cross-attention maps over text tokens from a source generation and limits their injection in time to permit structural changes ( Hertz et al., 2022 ) . SaaS identifies source-image dominance over neglected instructions in OmniGen and adaptively scales instruction attention. In its examples, jointly replacing image and text inputs late in denoising has little effect ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) . GRAG modulates the relative influence of source-image and instruction tokens to control editing intensity ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . We ask the same question about source conditioning, but instead of rescaling attention we change the conditioning inputs themselves and measure the outcome, using attention maps only as a diagnostic. Temporal conditioning. eDiff-I observes that reliance on text conditioning decreases during sampling and trains separate denoisers for different noise levels ( Balaji et al., 2022 ) . Restricting classifier-free guidance to a limited interval also improves generation ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ) . PCI intervenes on the text prompt during T2I sampling to find when a concept can still be inserted. The resulting temporal profiles differ across concepts and models and carry over to editing ( Görgün et al., 2026 ) . We extend this line of work from varying denoisers, guidance, or text prompts across denoising stages to switching between image-conditioned editing and caption-only generation within a unified model. Combining generation and editing. HiDream-E1’s released pipeline provides a direct precedent for an editing-to-generation handoff: it continues the same latent with a target caption, removes source-image conditioning, and finishes the remaining steps with the HiDream-I1 generator weights ( HiDream-ai, 2025 ) . For refinement of generated images, RvR argues that pixel-level preservation restricts the space of possible changes, and trains a regeneration model conditioned on target prompts and semantic image tokens without source VAE tokens ( Guo et al., 2026 ) . Building on these pipelines, we study how source-image conditioning, the text paired with it, and interval timing affect edit quality and source preservation across unified editors. Conditioning controls and timing sweeps use the models’ native editing and T2I modes within one denoising trajectory under unchanged weights. 3 Source conditioning along editing trajectories A unified model is trained for two tasks but runs one at a time. Every editing request has a source image, and the pipeline conditions on it at every step regardless of what the request asks for. Editing requests, however, differ widely in nature and in difficulty: enhancing the lighting adjusts an intact scene, whereas replacing a background asks the model to synthesize most of the image from scratch. It would be surprising if one conditioning policy served both equally well. This section examines how an editor actually uses the source image across such edits and across denoising steps. 3.1 Source attention varies across edits and timesteps If the source image matters more for some edits than for others, the most direct place to look is the model’s attention to it. We therefore measure how much each output patch attends to the source-image tokens during ordinary editing, and how that changes as denoising proceeds. We examine source attention along 50 50 -step pure-editing trajectories on FLUX2-Klein 4B. For each output latent patch i i , we sum attention over source-image tokens and average across heads and transformer blocks, obtaining a i a_{i} . At step k = 9 k=9 ( Figure 2 ), the three edits attend to the source very differently: only on the kept foreground for the background replacement, strongly everywhere for the lighting change, and weakly everywhere for the makeup look. How much the model uses the source depends on what the edit needs from it. Figure 2: Source attention varies across edits (FLUX2-Klein 4B, step 9). Maps average over heads and blocks. a i a_{i} @9 shows per-patch source attention; CV@9 shows the coefficient of variation in local 3 × 3 3\times 3 neighborhoods. Attention also changes over time ( Figure 3 a): source-attention mass generally decreases in the examined trajectories, whereas some local edits retain high attention through the final steps. The source image and instruction are identical at every step, so this variation reflects how the model uses fixed inputs. Where attention to the source has faded, conditioning on it constrains the model without contributing much. Since T2I generation is free of that constraint, we hypothesize that it can produce a better scene, and the question becomes where in the trajectory a T2I phase would disturb the edit the least. 3.2 Comparing editing and T2I predictions The two conditioning modes propose different updates to the same latent. Where they agree, switching between them changes little; where they diverge, a switch pulls the trajectory off the edit. To find the low-disturbance region, we compute both predictions at every step of an ordinary edit. At each latent state of a pure-editing trajectory, we compare predictions conditioned on the source image and instruction ( v E v_{\mathrm{E}} ) with predictions conditioned on a target caption ( v T2I v_{\mathrm{T2I}} ). Their directional agreement and norm ratio ( Figure 3 b,c) are highly variable early, comparatively stable in the middle, and diverge again late for local edits. This suggests that the effect of switching depends on its timing, so we test both one-way switches and bounded intervals placed in the stable middle region. The comparison is a diagnostic: it reads both predictions at each step without altering the sampled trajectory, whereas the switching schedules below evaluate one mode per step. Figure 3: Conditioning disagreement and source attention along pure editing (FLUX2-Klein 4B). (a) Source-attention mass generally decreases, while local edits retain high attention late in sampling. (b) Prediction cosine similarity, initially low (median 0.48 0.48 ). (c) T2I/edit prediction norm ratio. Both are evaluated at identical latent states. 3.3 Conditioning interventions and controls Table 1: Conditioning inputs. To test whether it helps, we intervene directly: for part of the trajectory we hand the latent to the model’s T2I mode and let it continue with a caption of the target scene, then return to editing. Edit conditioning E \mathrm{E} uses a source image x src x_{\mathrm{src}} and instruction p edit p_{\mathrm{edit}} ; T2I uses a target caption c tgt c_{\mathrm{tgt}} generated beforehand by a VLM from those inputs. A one-way switch E → T2I \mathrm{E}\to\mathrm{T2I} retains caption-only conditioning from step k k onward. A bounded schedule E → T2I → E \mathrm{E}\to\mathrm{T2I}\to\mathrm{E} uses it on [ k 1 , k 2 ) [k_{1},k_{2}) and edit conditioning elsewhere. Both continue denoising the same latent. Only one mode is active per step, so FLUX2-Klein 4B/9B still run the baseline’s two denoiser passes per step. The only overhead is one VLM call for the caption (timings in Appendix D ). Switching changes both image and text inputs. To separate their effects, we test the original instruction without the source image ( ∅ \varnothing ) and the target caption with the source image ( Table 1 ). The E ∗ \mathrm{E}^{*} control supplies a VLM-improved instruction p edit ∗ p_{\mathrm{edit}}^{*} , at the cost of the same single VLM call as caption generation. Outside the interval, the controls use ordinary edit conditioning. An additional control uses the target caption throughout and removes the source image only during the interval ( Table 7 ). Together, the schedules (when conditioning changes) and the controls (what it changes to) let us attribute any gain to the removal of the source image, the change of text, or their timing. 4 Effects of conditioning and interval timing To test whether the effect is a property of unified editors rather than of one model, we evaluate three that differ in size, architecture, and training: FLUX2-Klein 4B and 9B ( Black Forest Labs, 2025 ) , two sizes of one diffusion-transformer family, and BAGEL ( Deng et al., 2025 ) , a separately developed model. The benchmarks cover complementary aspects of editing quality. GEdit-Bench ( Liu et al., 2025 ) uses real user instructions across task types and scores semantic consistency and perceptual quality separately. ImgEdit ( Ye et al., 2025 ) adds hard categories such as extraction, composition, and actions. MagicBrush ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) supplies a reference caption for every target, which allows a judge-free alignment score. GIE-Bench ( Qian et al., 2025 ) scores functional correctness and preservation separately, so quality gains can be priced in preservation. Setup. All models run with unchanged weights and 50 50 steps ( k = 0 , … , 49 k=0,\ldots,49 ); target captions and improved instructions come from Gemini-2.5-pro by default ( Comanici et al., 2025 ) (Qwen3.5 captioners are compared in Appendix D ). GEdit is judged by GPT-4.1 ( OpenAI, 2025 ) on a 0 0 – 10 10 scale, ImgEdit by GPT-4o ( Hurst et al., 2024 ) on 1 1 – 5 5 , and GIE-Bench correctness by GPT-4o in % \% ; MagicBrush reports CLIP-T cosine similarity to the reference caption, and GIE-Bench preservation is SSIM outside the edit mask and whole-image Unmasked-CLIP similarity to the source. Per GEdit sample, semantic consistency (SC) is the minimum of fidelity and preservation, perceptual quality (PQ) the minimum of naturalness and artifact-free appearance, and overall O = SC ⋅ PQ O=\sqrt{\mathrm{SC}\cdot\mathrm{PQ}} ; scores are averaged within task types, then across types. The GEdit conditioning matrices and Figures 6 and 7 use Qwen3.5 ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) ; the extended 4B GIE-Bench sweep uses Gemini-3-Flash ( Google DeepMind, 2025 ) . Variability. Baseline standard deviations come from three seeds with one judge pass each, so they mix generation and judge variability. They describe the baseline only, and the uncertainty of the switching gains is assessed separately. Paired quality tests on 4B use two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and exact McNemar tests for binary correctness on matched per-edit records. Preservation comparisons are described in Appendix F . 4.1 Task switching improves editing quality Trading preservation for quality is easy: any editor can be pushed toward the target by loosening its anchor to the source. Improving quality without giving up preservation is the hard part, and this is what a T2I interval achieves. Our sweeps over interval length and position identify [ 10 , 16 ) [10,16) as a strong fixed interval: applied to every edit, it raises all six quality scores on all three models ( Table 2 ), while preservation as judged by GPT-4.1 stays within a fraction of a point of pure editing. The pixel-level measures, SSIM and Unmasked-CLIP, do drop, and Section 4.4 examines how much of that drop is perceptible. The interval is not unique: several placements improve GEdit semantic consistency and perceptual quality at once ( Figure 4 ), and which one is best depends on the model and the metric. We feature [ 10 , 16 ) [10,16) because it was consistently strong in the FLUX2-Klein 4B sweeps across all four benchmarks. On 9B and BAGEL we tested a smaller set of intervals, and [ 10 , 16 ) [10,16) again ranked among the strongest ( Figures 4 and 9 ), so we report it for all three models and use it for the selective variant. The interval was not re-tuned per model or benchmark. Full GIE-Bench, MagicBrush, and GEdit results are reported in Tables 3 , 4 and 5 . A one-way T2I switch can improve instruction fidelity while changing unrelated content; resuming edit conditioning after the interval limits these changes. 4.2 What accounts for the improvements? Image and text conditioning. Switching changes two things at once, the image input and the text, and the controls in Table 1 pull them apart; Table 8 summarizes the best scores for each conditioning schedule. Rewording alone does help: a VLM-improved instruction early in the trajectory reaches the highest GEdit overall score among the control winners ( Figure 7 , left). But the perceptual-quality gain is specific to removing the source image. With the same caption, comparing conditioning with and without the source image ( Figure 6 ) shows that removing the image allows larger gains in fidelity, naturalness, and artifact scores on every model. The text matters in two different ways. Removing the image while keeping only the editing instruction loses semantic consistency, because nothing tells the model what the scene should become. Pairing the caption with the source image also loses semantic consistency, whether the pair is used for the whole trajectory or only outside the interval; here the caption does describe the target, so the likely cause is that the editor was trained to combine the source image with an instruction, not with a description of the result. The improvement therefore comes from switching the task, source-free generation toward a described target, and not from either change alone. The strongest single competitor is the improved instruction used for the whole trajectory, pure E ∗ , which costs the same one VLM call and the same two denoiser passes per step as switching ( Table 10 ). It is a strong baseline on the two FLUX models, where it wins GEdit semantic consistency and keeps SSIM higher. But on every model the best T2I interval beats it on GIE-Bench functional correctness, MagicBrush alignment, and GEdit perceptual quality, and the perceptual-quality margin is large. Where E ∗ wins semantic consistency, it does so through the preservation part of that score; fidelity is matched or exceeded by the T2I interval. On BAGEL, the improved instruction alone does not help at all, while the T2I interval improves every quality score. Better prompts make the editor follow the instruction more faithfully; only switching makes the result look better. Figure 6: Removing the source image allows larger quality gains with the same caption (GEdit, Qwen3.5). Bands span per-metric extrema across switch timings, with and without a return to editing, so one band edge can combine several configurations. Axes normalized independently. Continuous guidance comparisons. Continuous guidance provides a natural alternative to switching. Reducing image guidance over the same intervals barely changes GEdit overall and lowers ImgEdit, because image-conditioned predictions still drive the update even at zero guidance. Adding a caption-conditioned branch instead blends edit and T2I velocities at every step. At a quarter editing weight, this improves semantic consistency, correctness, and preservation over the pure E → T2I → E \mathrm{E}\to\mathrm{T2I}\to\mathrm{E} switch, but requires four denoiser passes per step rather than two ( Appendix C ). Switching is the endpoint of this family at the cost of pure editing and captures most of the benefit. 4.3 When does switching help? Interval placement and duration are not independent knobs. Across all four durations, the sweeps trace one curve ( Figure 7 , right): moving an interval earlier or making it longer buys perceptual quality and spends semantic consistency, and every curve returns to the pure-editing point as the interval slides toward the end of the trajectory. What matters is how much of the trajectory is spent in T2I and how early. The semantic-consistency cost comes from its preservation half; because SC takes the per-sample minimum of fidelity and preservation, a fidelity gain is hidden whenever preservation drops further. Only short intervals in the early-middle of the trajectory land in the region that improves both scores, which is why [ 10 , 16 ) [10,16) is the featured setting. Beyond that region the choice is a trade: an editor that values naturalness should switch earlier or longer, one that values consistency later or shorter. Right: T2I sweeps by duration Δ ​ k \Delta k ; shading marks gains in both metrics. 4.4 Quality and source preservation The quality gains are not free, but the two kinds of preservation metric price them very differently. SSIM outside the edit mask and Unmasked-CLIP drop for every switching configuration, and significantly so ( Appendix F ). A judge asked only about unintended changes sees far less. We score preservation with GPT-4.1 using GEdit’s preservation criterion with the fidelity part removed, so the judge penalizes only changes that the instruction did not ask for ( Appendix F ). On this measure the fixed interval moves mean preservation by at most 0.16 0.16 points on a ten-point scale across the three models, and none of these shifts is significant. Figure 8 (right) puts the two sides together: the featured intervals gain correctness at judged preservation indistinguishable from pure editing, while the early one-way switches that gain the most correctness are the ones that pay for it. Withholding the interval from part of the edits ( Section 4.5 ) recovers a portion of the SSIM loss on every model and brings judged preservation closer still to pure editing. The two metrics disagree because they measure different things. Figure 8 (left) shows how far the pixel drop overstates the cost: across the 4B sweep, judged preservation forms a plateau at the pure-editing level while SSIM varies, and declines only below it. The attention signal identifies edits that can afford the interval. 5 Discussion and conclusion Unified editors are trained for two tasks but use one at a time; this study puts the unused mode to work within an edit. An editor’s attention to the source image depends on what the edit needs from it and fades over denoising for edits that rebuild the scene, leaving a stretch of the trajectory where source conditioning constrains without contributing. Switching to the model’s own T2I mode on that stretch improves edit quality on every model and benchmark we tested, while an instruction-aware judge finds preservation essentially unchanged. The gain is a property of the switch rather than of the prompt: removing the source image is what unlocks perceptual quality, the caption is what keeps the scene on target, and continuous guidance reproduces the effect only at twice the cost. Placement and duration set where on the quality–preservation curve an editor lands, and the same attention signal that motivated the study can decide per edit whether to switch at all. We use a simple switching schedule to establish that task switching can improve editing quality. More sophisticated switching and conditioning schemes may offer further gains. Our interval sweeps are coarse, so [ 10 , 16 ) [10,16) is one effective setting among those tested. A caption prepared before sampling cannot react to the trajectory, and its errors produce coherent but unintended changes. Preservation is measured by image similarity and a GPT judge, and how these track human judgments is untested.
